country.comment: The study examines the Zona Metropolitana del Valle de México (ZMVM) in Mexico, focusing on the relationship between Mexico City (CDMX) and peripheral municipalities of the State of Mexico (specifically the municipality of Ecatepec).

effect_estimate.comment: The paper conducts no inferential statistical testing; numeric figures come from descriptive mapping of secondary 2015 INEGI Intercensal data and cited secondary studies, combined with qualitative historical-institutional and hemerographic analysis.
effect_estimate.value: Qualitative / descriptive — no inferential numeric effect estimate reported. Descriptive analysis of 2015 INEGI Encuesta Intercensal data indicates that 81.39% of the ZMVM population had in-dwelling water access while 3 million people lacked potable water and drainage; in the Central Region and Contour 1 no municipality/alcaldía had less than 98% piped-water availability, whereas peripheral municipalities/alcaldías in Contours 3 and 4 (Tezoyuca, Tepetlixpa, Tequixquiac, Milpa Alta) had >10% of residents without piped water (and, citing González 2017, at least 15 peripheral Estado de México municipalities had <40% in-dwelling water access compared with only 2 of 16 CDMX alcaldías at 40-45%, despite ~30% of ZMVM water supply originating in the Estado de México). Neoinstitutional historical analysis and a hemerographic review of 7 water protests in Ecatepec (2018-2020) link peripheral water scarcity and supply cuts to territorial marginalization, unplanned irregular settlements lacking legal land title, incomplete intergovernmental decentralization (delegation and deconcentration without fiscal/technical autonomy), hydraulic centralization favoring CDMX, and partisan clientelist water allocation between state (CAEM) and municipal (SAPASE) authorities.

mechanism_certainty.comment: Rated 1 under CODEBOOK.md §9 (design ceiling <=2 for non-experimental/non-quasi-experimental designs). The study documents descriptive spatial disparities across metropolitan jurisdictions/contours using 2015 INEGI census data and compiles 7 newspaper-reported water-protest episodes in Ecatepec (2018-2020), while relying on secondary literature (e.g., González 2017; Hernández 2015; Pineda 2002) rather than direct primary empirical observation inside administrative or legal decision-making processes.

mechanism_flags.comment: Examines irregular land tenure without legal title (tenure) and unplanned peripheral growth (planning), core-periphery jurisdictional service prioritization (service_area), arbitrary/clientelist partisan water allocation and illicit fee charging by utility workers (discretion), divided state-municipal-federal water authority and incomplete fiscal decentralization following 1983 municipalization and the 2016 CDMX alcaldía reform (institutional_fragmentation, political_coordination), barriers to citizen participation and shift from clientelist gobernabilidad to participatory gobernanza (participation), and public protests/petitions to municipal, state, federal, and human-rights bodies (complaint).

outcome_flags.comment: Analyzes household access to water (water_access), connection/availability of piped public-network water versus reliance on tankers/wells (formal_connection), municipal/contour-level water coverage disparities (service_coverage), supply cuts and restoration demands in Ecatepec (service_continuity), and deficiencies in water quantity and potable quality (service_quantity, service_quality). Lack of drainage is briefly noted on PDF p. 9 (sanitation_access) alongside potable water.

risk_of_bias_tool.comment: The paper is an institutional-historical and neoinstitutional documentary governance study (analyzing historical hydraulic policy, constitutional/statutory frameworks, 1983 municipalization, the 2016 CDMX political-administrative reform, secondary census maps, and a 7-event newspaper archive table of protests) with no human-subject interviews, focus groups, or ethnographic fieldwork; it therefore fits the Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework for institutional-historical studies.

sample_size.comment: No primary household survey or interview sample was collected; empirical scope consists of a qualitative case study of 1 municipality (Ecatepec) tracking 7 newspaper-documented protest events (2018-2020) and descriptive spatial mapping of secondary 2015 INEGI Intercensal data across the 76 municipalities/boroughs of the ZMVM.
sample_size.value: 1 case-study municipality (Ecatepec, 1,645,000 inhabitants in INEGI 2020) with 7 water-protest events in 2018-2020 hemerographic review (Table 1); descriptive secondary census mapping across 76 municipalities/boroughs of the Zona Metropolitana del Valle de México (16 CDMX delegaciones/alcaldías, 59 Estado de México municipalities, and 1 Hidalgo municipality; 20,892,724 inhabitants in INEGI 2015 Encuesta Intercensal)

study_design.comment: Authors describe the study as an analysis based on primary documentary sources from a neoinstitutional and historical perspective, combining descriptive spatial mapping of secondary 2015 INEGI Intercensal housing data across ZMVM contours with a newspaper-archive (hemerographic) case study of water protests in Ecatepec (2018-2020).
study_design.value: Institutional-historical and neoinstitutional documentary study with descriptive secondary census spatial mapping (INEGI 2015) and a qualitative hemerographic case study of municipal water protests (Ecatepec, 2018-2020)
